testimonials.text: The most interesting aspect of the course was learning how to recognise different pelvic fracture patterns and understand their anatomical significance. I particularly found the use of radiographic landmarks, such as the ilioischial and iliopectineal lines, helpful. The principles of managing haemodynamically unstable patients, especially the importance of simultaneous resuscitation, pelvic stabilisation and haemorrhage control, were also particularly valuable.

I found the most interesting aspect of this course to be its focus on the early, high-stakes management of pelvic fractures, especially how ATLS principles, pelvic ring stability, and hemorrhage control come together in real time. The idea that management is not purely sequential but requires simultaneous resuscitation, stabilization, and bleeding control was especially valuable.

I found the case presentations most interesting. Seeing real pelvic fracture cases from different parts of the world made the content practical and easy to understand. The discussion on managing unstable patients with a concurrent approach was also very useful.

I found the practice, case-based discussion around early resuscitation and concurrent management of haemodynamically unstable pelvic fracture patient the most interesting. Learning to interpret pelvic radiographic lines and differentiate acetabular column anatomy was also engaging.

Learning how trauma teams prioritize resuscitation, pelvic stabilization, and hemorrhage control at the same time gave me a much better understanding of how quickly these injuries can become life-threatening.

The case-based discussions, imaging interpretation, and practical approach to pelvic fracture classification and acute management were the most engaging. They helped connect the theory to real clinical practice.

I found the sections on pelvic fracture classification and the correlation between radiographic landmark lines (iliopectineal, ilioischial) and the anatomical columns of the acetabulum particularly interesting. The case-based approach to hemodynamically unstable patients, especially the emphasis on the concurrent management of resuscitation, mechanical stabilization, and hemorrhage control, gave me a much clearer picture of how trauma protocols work in real clinical practice.
